subject: math
intro: Hi! I'm Ms. Rivera. Let's plan a 6th grade lesson on ratios — I'll talk you through each choice as I go.

beats.narration: I like titles that hint at the real-world hook. Kids remember "the recipe lesson."
I anchor to the standard first so every section has something to line up against.
My objective is observable: I can hear it and see it on paper by the end of class.
beats.text: Students will be able to use ratio language to describe the relationship between two quantities and write ratios three ways (a:b, a to b, a/b).

beats.narration: The warm-up surfaces the idea of "keeping it the same" before I ever say the word ratio.
beats.text: Show a photo of a lemonade recipe (3 cups water, 1 cup lemon juice). Ask: "If I want to make a bigger batch that tastes the same, what has to stay the same?" Turn and talk for 2 minutes.

beats.narration: I model with something in the room so the ratios are about things they can count right now.
beats.text: Model ratio language with the class seating chart: "For every 2 students at a window seat, there are 5 at an inside seat." Write it as 2:5, 2 to 5, and 2/5. Contrast part-to-part vs. part-to-whole.

beats.narration: Swapping bags builds in peer checking, so I can circulate and listen instead of grading everything.
beats.text: In pairs, students sort a bag of colored tiles and write four ratio statements about it — at least one part-to-whole. Partners swap bags and check each other's statements.

beats.narration: The exit ticket mirrors the objective exactly, so tomorrow I know who to pull into a small group.
beats.text: A class has 12 girls and 15 boys. Write the ratio of girls to boys and of boys to all students. Explain which one is part-to-whole.

outro: That's the whole plan — objective, hook, modeling, practice, and a quick check. Now it's your turn.
